title: Weak-equivalence spans give a Bergner path object for a chunk
statement:
Use combinatorial simplicial model categories and their model cofibrations, fibrations and weak equivalences as in [lem-coef-simplicial-projective-model-calculus], full chunks as in [lem-coef-simplicial-small-chunks], and the Bergner model structure on simplicial categories as in [lem-coef-coherent-nerve-comparison]. Let $\mathcal A$ be a combinatorial simplicial model category and $U\subseteq\mathcal A$ a full chunk. Set $U^{cf}=U\cap\mathcal A^{cf}$. Enlarge the ambient universe to contain every displayed category. Define a simplicial category $P(U)$ whose objects are triples $Z,B,C\in U^{cf}$ with a fibration $(p,q):Z\to B\times C$ such that $p$ and $q$ are weak equivalences. Its mapping simplicial set from $(Z\xrightarrow{(p,q)}B\times C)$ to $(Z'\xrightarrow{(p',q')}B'\times C')$ is the simplicial set of triples $(a,b,c)$ in $\underline{\operatorname{Map}}_{\mathcal A}(Z,Z')\times\underline{\operatorname{Map}}_{\mathcal A}(B,B')\times\underline{\operatorname{Map}}_{\mathcal A}(C,C')$ satisfying $p'a=bp$ and $q'a=cq$; composition and identities are componentwise. Write $\pi_0,\pi_1:P(U)\to U^{cf}$ for the functors selecting $B,C$ respectively.

The enriched functorial chunk factorization of $\Delta_B:B\to B\times B$ as a trivial cofibration $B\to Z_B$ followed by a fibration defines $\tau:U^{cf}\to P(U)$. These functors satisfy $\pi_0\tau=\pi_1\tau=1_{U^{cf}}$, the functor $\tau$ is a Dwyer--Kan equivalence, and $(\pi_0,\pi_1):P(U)\to U^{cf}\times U^{cf}$ is a Bergner fibration. Thus this is a path object for $U^{cf}$ in the Bergner model category: a factorization of its diagonal as a weak equivalence followed by a fibration. No cofibrancy of $U^{cf}$ is assumed.

source.place: Notation A.3.4.7 and Theorem A.3.4.8, printed pp.886-888 (PDF pp.903-905, zero-based pages). Read online 2026-10-17; not archived in literature/. No Stacks tag states the enriched chunk path-object theorem.

proof.text: Put $T=U^{cf}$ and write $M(X,Y)=\underline{\operatorname{Map}}_{\mathcal A}(X,Y)$. We use the following immediate consequences of the model weak factorization systems: right lifting classes are closed under pullback and composition (pull back a lifting problem, or solve its two successive lifting problems), and left lifting classes under composition by the dual argument. In particular, products of fibrant objects are fibrant: the product projection is a pullback of a terminal fibration. For $B\in T$, apply chunk property (a) to the two identity maps of $B$, obtaining $B\xrightarrow{j_B}Z_B\xrightarrow{r_B}B\times B$. The object $Z_B$ lies in $U$, is cofibrant since $j_B$ is a cofibration with cofibrant source, and is fibrant since $r_B$ is a fibration with fibrant target. Each component $r_{B,i}$ is weak because $r_{B,i}j_B=1_B$ and $j_B$ is weak. Thus $r_B$ is an object of $P(U)$. The enriched functoriality in the chunk definition gives the specified enriched $\tau$. Strict componentwise composition preserves the two displayed commutativity equations defining the mapping sets of $P(U)$, so these equations define a simplicial category and enriched endpoint functors. The two identities $\pi_0\tau=\pi_1\tau=1_T$ follow on objects and all mapping simplices from the functorial factorization.

source.place: Notation A.3.4.7 and Theorem A.3.4.8, printed pp.886-888; simplicial-set specialization of the proof.

proof.text: For objects $x=(Z\xrightarrow{(p,q)}B\times C)$ and $y=(Z'\xrightarrow{(p',q')}B'\times C')$ of $P(U)$, put $E=M(B,B')\times M(C,C')$, $D=M(Z,B')\times M(Z,C')$, and $F=M(Z,Z')$. The defining equations give the strict pullback formula $M_{P(U)}(x,y)=E\times_DF$, with $v:E\to D$ given by $(b,c)\mapsto(bp,cq)$ and $u:F\to D$ given by $a\mapsto(p'a,q'a)$. Here mapping into the product identifies $D$ with $M(Z,B'\times C')$. SM7, applied to the cofibration $\varnothing\to Z$ and the fibration $(p',q')$, says that $u$ is a Kan fibration. Its pullback to $E$ is exactly the local mapping map of $(\pi_0,\pi_1)$, so this local map is a Kan fibration. All the individual $M(X,Y)$ displayed here are Kan by SM7 for $\varnothing\to X$ and $Y\to *$, since all six objects are bifibrant; consequently $E,D,F$ are Kan. Products of Kan complexes are Kan by filling each horn coordinatewise; pulling back the fibration $u$ shows that $M_{P(U)}(x,y)$ is Kan too.

source.place: Notation A.3.4.7 and Theorem A.3.4.8, printed pp.886-888; simplicial-set specialization of the proof.

proof.text: The precomposition maps $p^*:M(B,B')\to M(Z,B')$ and $q^*:M(C,C')\to M(Z,C')$ are weak homotopy equivalences. Indeed the natural derived-mapping comparison identifies each with precomposition by the image of the corresponding model weak equivalence in the infinity localization. That image is invertible. Composing with an inverse gives a homotopy inverse on mapping spaces: associativity and the inverse equations identify both composites with the identity, using the composition and unit homotopies of [lem-coef-infinity-mapping-composition]. Thus both precomposition maps are equivalences of spaces. The same is true of $v=p^*\times q^*$: factor it as $p^*\times1$ followed by $1\times q^*$; each is the pullback of a weak equivalence along a product projection of Kan complexes, which is a Kan fibration, and apply right properness twice. Since $u$ is a Kan fibration, right properness now applied to $v$ shows that the pullback projection $k:E\times_DF\to F$ is a weak homotopy equivalence.

source.place: Notation A.3.4.7 and Theorem A.3.4.8, printed pp.886-888; simplicial-set specialization of the proof.

proof.text: The component $p':Z'\to B'$ is a fibration: it is the composite of $(p',q')$ and $B'\times C'\to B'$, the latter being a pullback of the terminal fibration of $C'$. It is weak by the definition of the objects of $P(U)$, hence a trivial fibration. Applying SM7 to $\varnothing\to Z$ and $p'$ shows that $p'_*:F\to M(Z,B')$ is a trivial Kan fibration. Let $r:E\times_DF\to M(B,B')$ be the first endpoint mapping map. The equality $p^*r=p'_*k$ follows from $p'a=bp$. The right side is a weak equivalence by Step 3 and the preceding SM7 application; $p^*$ is weak by Step 3, so two-out-of-three gives that $r$ is weak. This proves that $\pi_0:P(U)\to T$ is locally a weak homotopy equivalence.

source.place: Notation A.3.4.7 and Theorem A.3.4.8, printed pp.886-888; simplicial-set specialization of the proof.

proof.text: A weak homotopy equivalence of mapping sets gives a bijection on components. Thus Step 4 says that $\pi_0$ is fully faithful on component categories; it is essentially surjective because its strict section $\tau$ hits every object of $T$. Therefore $\pi_0$ is a Dwyer--Kan equivalence. The equation $\pi_0\tau=1_T$ and two-out-of-three for Bergner weak equivalences imply that $\tau$ is also a Dwyer--Kan equivalence. In particular the functor on component categories induced by $\pi_0$ reflects isomorphisms: lift the inverse of the image by fullness, and use faithfulness to check both inverse equations.

source.place: Notation A.3.4.7 and Theorem A.3.4.8, printed pp.886-888; simplicial-set specialization of the proof.

proof.text: For bifibrant objects $X,Y$ of $\mathcal A$ in $U$, a vertex $f:X\to Y$ is invertible in $\pi_0T$ if and only if it is a model weak equivalence. To check both implications without assuming $U$ closed under weak-equivalence zigzags, use the natural mapping-space representation for bifibrant objects and its compatibility with composition. It identifies $\pi_0T$ with the full subcategory on these objects in the component category of the infinity localization. An invertible component is an equivalence edge by [lem-coef-infinity-mapping-composition]. The image of a model weak equivalence is an equivalence by the defining property of localization, proving one implication. Conversely choose an ordinary localization $\gamma:\mathcal A\to\mathcal H$ at the model weak equivalences, enlarging universes as allowed. Its nerve factors through the infinity localization: this is the universal property applied with target $N\mathcal H$, because $\gamma$ sends weak equivalences to isomorphisms. Hence an equivalence image of $f$ maps to an isomorphism $\gamma(f)$. The detection theorem now implies that $f$ is a model weak equivalence.

source.place: Notation A.3.4.7 and Theorem A.3.4.8, printed pp.886-888; simplicial-set specialization of the proof.

proof.text: Consider the equivalence-lifting requirement for $(\pi_0,\pi_1)$ at $x=(Z,p,q)$, with target object $(B_1,C_1)$ of $T\times T$. Represent the specified two invertible component classes by vertices $f:B\to B_1$ and $g:C\to C_1$ of the corresponding mapping sets. Step 6 says that these actual maps are weak equivalences. Apply chunk property (a) to $fp:Z\to B_1$ and $gq:Z\to C_1$, giving $Z\xrightarrow{j}Z_1\xrightarrow{(p_1,q_1)}B_1\times C_1$ with $j$ a trivial cofibration, $(p_1,q_1)$ a fibration, and $Z_1\in U$. As in Step 1, $Z_1$ is cofibrant and fibrant. Since $p_1j=fp$ and $q_1j=gq$, two-out-of-three says that $p_1,q_1$ are weak. We therefore obtain $y=(Z_1,p_1,q_1)\in P(U)$ and the morphism $\alpha=(j,f,g):x\to y$, with endpoints exactly $f,g$. Its first endpoint is invertible in $\pi_0T$ by Step 6. The fully faithful functor on components of Step 5 reflects isomorphisms, so $[\alpha]$ is invertible in $\pi_0P(U)$. This is the required lift, even for a chosen representative vertex rather than merely its component.

source.place: Notation A.3.4.7 and Theorem A.3.4.8, printed pp.886-888; simplicial-set specialization of the proof.

proof.text: Step 2 verifies the local Kan-fibration condition for $(\pi_0,\pi_1)$, and Step 7 verifies its equivalence-lifting condition. These are exactly the two conditions for a Bergner fibration. Together with Step 5 and the strict endpoint identities of Step 1, this gives the required factorization of the diagonal of $T$ as a Bergner weak equivalence followed by a Bergner fibration. All constructions used only the objectwise cofibrancy and fibrancy inside $T$, never cofibrancy of the simplicial category $T$. If $U$ is empty then $T,P(U)$ are empty, the mapping and lifting conditions are vacuous, and the same conclusion holds.

lean.statement: theorem chunk_span_path_object {A : Type w} [Category.{u} A] [ModelCategory A] [SimplicialCategory A] (_T : SimplicialTensorCotensor A) (_hC : CombinatorialModelCategory.{w, u, u} A) (_hSM7 : SimplicialModelLocalization.SatisfiesSM7 A) (U : SimplicialChunk A) : ∃ (D : EnrichedFunctor SSet.{u} U.cf.FullSubcategory (productFamilies U.carrier 2).FullSubcategory) (τ : EnrichedFunctor SSet.{u} U.cf.FullSubcategory (Spans U)) (π₀ π₁ : EnrichedFunctor SSet.{u} (Spans U) U.cf.FullSubcategory), (∀ B, D.obj B = diagonalFamily U B) ∧ (∀ B C j, HEq (D.map B C ≫ enrichedHomπ SSet (D.obj B).obj (D.obj C).obj j) (𝟙 (sHom B C))) ∧ (∀ B, (τ.obj B).obj = diagonalSpan U B) ∧ (∀ B C, HEq (τ.map B C ≫ enrichedHomπ SSet (τ.obj B).obj (τ.obj C).obj none) (D.map B C ≫ (U.product_factorization 2).middle.map (D.obj B) (D.obj C))) ∧ (∀ x, (π₀.obj x).obj = x.obj.obj (some 0)) ∧ (∀ x, (π₁.obj x).obj = x.obj.obj (some 1)) ∧ (∀ x y, HEq (π₀.map x y) (enrichedHomπ SSet x.obj y.obj (some 0))) ∧ (∀ x y, HEq (π₁.map x y) (enrichedHomπ SSet x.obj y.obj (some 1))) ∧ τ.comp SSet π₀ = EnrichedFunctor.id SSet U.cf.FullSubcategory ∧ τ.comp SSet π₁ = EnrichedFunctor.id SSet U.cf.FullSubcategory ∧ DwyerKanEquivalence τ ∧ (∀ x y, SSet.modelCategoryQuillen.J.rlp (CartesianMonoidalCategory.lift (π₀.map x y) (π₁.map x y))) ∧ (∀ (x : Spans U) (B C : U.cf.FullSubcategory) (f : π₀.obj x ⟶ B) (g : π₁.obj x ⟶ C), IsPiZeroIso f → IsPiZeroIso g → ∃ (y : Spans U) (a : x ⟶ y) (h₀ : π₀.obj y = B) (h₁ : π₁.obj y = C), IsPiZeroIso a ∧ SSet.π₀.mk (homEquiv' _ _ ((eHomEquiv SSet).symm (eHomEquiv SSet a ≫ π₀.map x y) ≫ eqToHom h₀)) = SSet.π₀.mk (homEquiv' _ _ f) ∧ SSet.π₀.mk (homEquiv' _ _ ((eHomEquiv SSet).symm (eHomEquiv SSet a ≫ π₁.map x y) ≫ eqToHom h₁)) = SSet.π₀.mk (homEquiv' _ _ g))
